To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a cumulative measure (allostatic load) of multiple physiological dysregulations, reflecting multiple regulatory systems (e.g., cardiovascular, metabolic, immune), is associated with mortality risk in the elderly, and that this measure accounts for a significant portion of the SES differences in mortality risk.
SES differences in mortality can be partially mediated by a cumulative measure of multiple regulatory systems.

Cumulative biological dysregulation, reflecting multiple regulatory systems and processes, explains a significant proportion of the education-related variation in all-cause mortality among older adults.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the mechanisms through which socio-economic differences in morbidity and mortality are mediated, and suggests that a cumulative index reflecting multiple physiological systems is a useful tool for furthering our understanding of this issue.
the biological pathways by which SES differences in morbidity and mortality are mediated, with a focus on cumulative biological risk as a mediator of SES differences.
understanding the pathways through which socio-economic differences in morbidity and mortality arise and with developing a more complete understanding of biological mechanisms that may be involved.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a cumulative measure, which reflects multiple physiological dysregulations, is a significant mediator of the association between SES and mortality.
the cumulative measure of biological risk is a better predictor of mortality than any individual measure of biological risk and is a better predictor than the measure of chronic disease.
a cumulative index based on multiple biological systems provides a more comprehensive measure of SES-related mortality differences than do single indicators of biological risk.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SES is related to mortality risk, and the relationship is mediated by biological dysregulation.

the cumulative biological risk index, which is an indicator of the cumulative impact of multiple biological systems, is a significant mediator of the relationship between SES and mortality, even when controlling for doctor-diagnosed illness.
SES differences in mortality are mediated by both life-style factors and biological dysregulation, with the latter being a potentially more powerful mediator than the former.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of SES on health and well-being are not limited to the social and behavioral domains.
the cumulative index of biological dysregulations is a useful summary measure for understanding the biological underpinnings of socio-economic differences in health outcomes.

the cumulative biological risk index, as measured in the MacArthur Study, is an independent predictor of mortality and accounts for a significant proportion of the mortality differences between those with less than a high school education and those with a high school education or greater.
